Transformers know more than they can tell
Learning the Collatz sequence

François Charton francois@axiommath.ai Affiliation: Axiom Math Affiliation: CERMICS, Ecole Nationale des Ponts et Chaussées    Ashvni Narayanan ashvni.narayanan@sydney.edu.au Affiliation: Sydney Mathematical Research Institute, University of Sydney
Abstract

We investigate transformer prediction of long Collatz steps, a complex arithmetic function that maps odd integers to their distant successors in the Collatz sequence ( un+1=un/2u_{n+1}=u_{n}/2 if unu_{n} is even, un+1=(3​un+1)/2u_{n+1}=(3u_{n}+1)/2 if unu_{n} is odd). Model accuracy varies with the base used to encode input and output. It can be as high as 99.7%99.7\% for bases 2424 and 3232, and as low as 3737 and 25%25\% for bases 1111 and 33. Yet, all models, no matter the base, follow a common learning pattern. As training proceeds, they learn a sequence of classes of inputs that share the same residual modulo 2p2^{p}. Models achieve near-perfect accuracy on these classes, and less than 1%1\% for all other inputs. This maps to a mathematical property of Collatz sequences: the length of the loops involved in the computation of a long Collatz step can be deduced from the binary representation of its input. The learning pattern reflects the model learning to predict inputs associated with increasing loop lengths. An analysis of failure cases reveals that almost all model errors follow predictable patterns. Hallucination, a common feature of large language models, almost never happens. In over 90%90\% of failures, the model performs the correct calculation, but wrongly estimates loop lengths. Our observations give a full account of the algorithms learned by the models. They suggest that the difficulty of learning such complex arithmetic function lies in figuring the control structure of the computation – the length of the loops. We believe that the approach outlined here, using mathematical problems as tools for understanding, explaining, and perhaps improving language models, can be applied to a broad range of problems and bear fruitful results.

1 Introduction

Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017), the prevalent architecture in deep learning models (Radford et al., 2019; Touvron et al., 2023; the Gemini Team, 2025), prove surprisingly weak when trained on simple arithmetic operations (Lee et al., 2023; Hanna et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021). Learning long integer addition, a basic operation, requires advanced techniques, such as scratchpads (Nye et al., 2021) or chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2023). Generalizing to larger (or smaller) operands that those used during training requires problem-specific positional embeddings (McLeish et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2023). In many recent models, integer multiplication fails unless one of the operands is small (Qiu et al., 2024; Dziri et al., 2023), and complex arithmetic operations cannot be learned (Lee et al., 2023). These limitations are all the more shocking as transformers have been used to solve hard problems of mathematics, such as symbolic integration (Lample and Charton, 2019), discovering Lyapunov functions and Gröbner bases (Alfarano et al., 2024; Kera et al., 2024; Kambe et al., 2025), or finding new solutions to old problems in combinatorics (Charton et al., 2024; Ellenberg et al., 2025).

Workarounds have been proposed, such as interfacing with external tools (Schick et al., 2023) or generating computer code that performs the calculations (Romera-Paredes et al., 2023). Theoretical papers have also investigated the limitations of transformer architectures when performing exact computations on very long sequences (Zhou et al., 2023; Weiss et al., 2021). Still, little is understood about why transformers struggle with arithmetic tasks, and how such functions are learned, from examples only. Prior works focus on small models and simple operations, such as modular addition (Zhong et al., 2023; Nanda et al., 2023), the Möbius function (Lowry-Duda, 2025), or the greatest common divisor (Charton, 2024b).

In this paper, we train small transformers to learn a complex arithmetic function, the long Collatz step (Sec. 3): predicting a distant successor in the Collatz sequence (un+1=(3​un+1)/2u_{n+1}=(3u_{n}+1)/2 if unu_{n} is odd, un+1=un/2u_{n+1}=u_{n}/2 if unu_{n} is even). We chose this particular function for a number of reasons. First, the Collatz sequence, despite having a very simple definition, is known to give rise to complex mathematical behavior. Because it is the subject of a longstanding conjecture, it was heavily researched. We will leverage this prior knowledge when designing and interpreting our experiments. Second, the algorithm for computing the long Collatz step features two loops of variable length. This is a much more complex task than the basic arithmetic operations studied in prior works. Finally, as its input varies, the long Collatz step takes a lot of different values (23.523.5 million different values over the 5050 million first odd integers). Prior works focused on functions with a small number of outcomes. Learning such functions amount to a pattern recognition problem: mapping inputs onto a small number of classes. Learning the long Collatz step, on the other hand, amounts to a regression problem, a harder setting for learning machines.

We compare models using different bases to represent integers (Sec. 4). The best models (bases 2424, 1616 and 3232) achieve a near-perfect accuracy of 99.7%99.7\%, while odd-base models struggle to get past 80%80\%. Yet, all models learn the long Collatz step in a sequence of discrete steps, where specific classes of input are learned and predicted with very high accuracy (Sec. 4.1). This learning pattern is independent of the base, and corresponds to a deep mathematical property of the Collatz sequence: the structure of a long Collatz step, the length of the loops involved in its computation, can be deduced from the binary representation of its input (Sec. 4.2).

An investigation of model errors (Section 5) reveals that, whereas large language models commonly “hallucinate” random solutions, our models fail in principled ways. In almost all cases, the models perform the correct calculations for the long Collatz step, but use the wrong loop lengths, by setting them to the longest loop lengths they have learned so far. This unites model errors and the learning pattern, and provides a full account of the algorithm learned by our models. It also suggests that the hardness of the task does not lie in learning the arithmetic operations but in figuring the control structures of the algorithm, the lengths of the loops, which can be deduced from the binary representation of the input.

These results shed light on the learning patterns at work in math transformers. They confirm that, when learning the long Collatz steps, models do not rely on shortcuts or shallow statistical properties of the task, but learn deep mathematical properties of the problem, which allow¡ them to perform better than their accuracy figure suggest, that is, fail in principled ways instead of hallucinating. We believe that the method we propose to investigate the long Collatz step can be applied to many problems, and help understand how transformers learn mathematics.

2 Related works

Neural networks were first applied to problems of arithmetic in the early 1990s (Siu and Roychowdhury, 1992). Recurrent architectures (precursors of the transformer) were proposed by Zaremba et al. (2015), Kalchbrenner et al. (2015), and Kaiser and Sutskever (2015). Recent research mostly focuses on fine-tuning large pre-trained transformers on arithmetic tasks, to solve math word problems (Meng and Rumshisky, 2019; Griffith and Kalita, 2021). The hardness of arithmetic was first observed by Saxton et al. (2019). For a survey of the limitations of transformers on arithmetic tasks, see Lee et al. (2023) and Dziri et al. (2023).

Long integer addition received most of the attention. Scratchpad methods, that allow transformers to add long integer, were proposed by Nye et al. (2021). The importance of base representation was discussed by Nogueira et al. (2021). Length generalization, adding longer (or shorter) integers than those in the training set was discussed by Jelassi et al. (2023), and addressed by McLeish et al. (2024), via a task-specific positional embedding.

Modular and finite field arithmetic was investigated in the context of grokking (Power et al., 2022), delayed generalization of overfitted models (Gromov, 2023; Nanda et al., 2023), and cryptography (Wenger et al., 2022). In Saxena et al. (2025) and  Charton (2024a), we propose losses, embeddings and training techniques to help learn such tasks.

In Charton (2024b), we train transformers to predict the greatest common divisor (GCD) of two integers, a basic arithmetic operation with a small number of possible outcomes. The methodology is very close to ours: small transformers trained on randomly generated examples, using different bases to encode integers. Models learn to cluster their input pairs into classes sharing a common divisor, a learning pattern similar to ours. However, the pattern depends on the encoding base. Adjusting the training distribution, by oversampling small operands and large outcomes, brings a large improvement in model performance, a phenomenon we do not observe for the long Collatz steps (Section 6.3).

Most prior work on math transformer interpretability focuses on model weights (Nanda et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2023). Methods similar to ours were proposed for linear algebra (Charton, 2022), and the GCD (Charton, 2024b).

The Collatz conjecture (all Collatz sequences eventually reach 11), also known as the 3x+1 problem, Ulam conjecture, Kakutani’s problem, Thwaites conjecture, or the Syracuse problem, was proposed by Collatz in 1937, when he was a student. It is often cited as an example of a very hard problem with a very simple statement, and was heavily studied (Lagarias, 2021, for a summary). It holds true for all starting numbers up to 2712^{71}.

Many generalizations of the Collatz conjecture have been proposed: to positive reals  (Konstadinidis, 2006), with different constants (Bruschi, 2008), over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} (Gallardo and Rahavandrainy, 2023), in polynomial rings over commutative rings (Behajaina and Paran, 2024), to rationals with odd numerators and denominators  (Kobus, 2025). It is related to other hard problems, such as the ABC conjecture (Rozier, 2025), Terras’ conjecture (Rozier and Terracol, 2025), and the existence of special additive systems in ℤ\mathbb{Z} (Zabolotskii, 2025).

Recent attempts at proving the Collatz conjecture used dynamical systems (Siegel, 2024; Fu and Wang, 2025; Dominici, 2007), operator theory  (Mori, 2025) and graph theory  (Andrei et al., 2000). Tao (2022), using a probabilistic argument, proved that almost all Collatz orbits attain almost bounded values.

3 Long Collatz steps

The Collatz sequence 𝒞⁡(n)\mathcal{C}(n) associated with a positive integer nn is defined as:

c0\displaystyle c_{0} =n,\displaystyle=n,
ci+1\displaystyle c_{i+1} =ci2,if ci is even (a down-step),\displaystyle=\frac{c_{i}}{2},\text{if $c_{i}$ is even (a \emph{down-step}),}
ci+1\displaystyle c_{i+1} =3​ci+12,if ci is odd (an up-step).\displaystyle=\frac{3c_{i}+1}{2},\text{if $c_{i}$ is odd (an \emph{up-step}).}

𝒞⁡(1)\mathcal{C}(1), the Collatz sequence associated to 11 is the infinitely repeating loop (1,2,1)(1,2,1). It is conjectured that any Collatz sequence 𝒞⁡(n)\mathcal{C}(n) eventually reaches 11.

Assume nn is odd, and let 2k2^{k} be the largest power of two dividing n+1n+1, that is, n=2k​m−1n=2^{k}m-1 with mm odd and k≥1k\geq 1. Since c0=nc_{0}=n is odd, c1=3​n+12=2k−1​(3​m)−1,c_{1}=\frac{3n+1}{2}=2^{k-1}(3m)-1, an odd integer if k>1k>1. Repeating this kk times, we have.

Property 3.1.

Any odd positive integer of the form n=2k​m−1n=2^{k}m-1, with k≥1k\geq 1 and mm odd, is transformed, after kk Collatz up-steps, into ck=3k​m−1,c_{k}=3^{k}m-1, an even positive integer.

Let k′≥1k^{\prime}\geq 1 be the largest power of two dividing ckc_{k}, i.e. ck=2k′​pc_{k}=2^{k^{\prime}}p with pp odd. The next k′k^{\prime} steps of the Collatz sequences will be division by 22 (down-steps), and we have

ck+k′=3k​m−12k′=(32)k​(n+1)−12k′.c_{k+k^{\prime}}=\frac{3^{k}m-1}{2^{k^{\prime}}}=\frac{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{k}(n+1)-1}{2^{k^{\prime}}}.

We call this sequence of k+k′k+k^{\prime} Collatz steps a long Collatz step, and define, for any odd n=2k​m−1n=2^{k}m-1, its long Collatz successor11 1 We could define the long Collatz successor of an even integer as κ⁡(2k​m)=m.\kappa(2^{k}m)=m. as

κ⁡(n)=(32)k​(n+1)−12k′.\kappa(n)=\frac{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{k}(n+1)-1}{2^{k^{\prime}}}.

The long Collatz step transforms an odd integer into an odd integer. It has 11 as a fixed point, the only one if the Collatz conjecture is true.

To compute κ⁡(n)\kappa(n) for a given nn, one first applies kk times the transformation n→3​n+12n\to\frac{3n+1}{2}, then k′k^{\prime} times n→n2n\to\frac{n}{2}. kk and k′k^{\prime} are functions of nn. kk is the largest power of two that divides n+1n+1, i.e. the number of ones at the right of the binary representation of nn. k′k^{\prime} is the largest power of two dividing ck=3k​m−1=(32)k​(n+1)−1c_{k}=3^{k}m-1={(\frac{3}{2})}^{k}(n+1)-1, the apex aa of the long Collatz step.

Therefore, the algorithm for computing the long Collatz step involves two loops of variable length. If we know the binary representation of nn and aa, or can test the parity of intermediary results, we can compute κ⁡(n)\kappa(n) with one of the two algorithms below.

4 Learning the long Collatz step

We train transformers to predict κ⁡(n)\kappa(n), the long Collatz successor of nn, from a large set of pairs (n,κ⁡(n))(n,\kappa(n)), with nn odd, uniformly drawn between 11 and 101210^{12}. Our models are sequence-to-sequence transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017), with a bidirectional encoder, with 44 layers, an embedding dimension of 512512, and 88 attention heads, and an autoregressive decoder with 11 layer, a dimension of 512512 and 88 heads, connected to the encoder by a cross-attention mechanism.

Model inputs and outputs are encoded as sequences of digits in base BB. We train 5656 models, for all bases from 22 to 5757, on about 300300 million random pairs (n,κ⁡(n))(n,\kappa(n)). Models minimize a cross-entropy loss, using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 3⋅10−53\cdot 10^{-5}.

At regular intervals (every 300,000 training examples, an “epoch” henceforth), model accuracies are measured on a test set of 100,000 random pairs, as the percentage of exact predictions of κ⁡(n)\kappa(n). The large size of the problem space (5⋅10115\cdot 10^{11} possible values of nn) guarantees that there is almost no overlap between training and test set.

Table 1 summarize trained model accuracies. The best performing models, using base 2424, 1616 and 3232, achieve 99.7%99.7\% accuracy, a surprising result given the complexity of the task and the low performance of arithmetic transformers reported in prior works (Lee et al., 2023; Charton, 2024b). Performance varies with the base: all even-base models achieve 88%88\% accuracy or more. Most odd-base models are below 80%80\% accuracy. Accuracies tend to concentrate around a small set of values: of the 2828 odd base models, 1212 achieve 51%51\% accuracy, 88 achieve 55%55\% and 44 achieve 81%81\%.

The learning curves (Figure 1) confirm this phenomenon. Learning happens in steps, as model accuracies jump from one level to the next. These accuracy levels are quantized: they take the same values for all bases. As training proceeds, all odd-base model accuracies step from 25%25\% to 3737, 5555, 7171 and sometimes 81%81\%. Even-base model step from 71%71\% accuracy to 8181, 8888 and 92%92\%. This learning pattern is intriguing. Step-like learn curves were observed in prior works on arithmetic (Charton, 2024b), but accuracy levels varied with the base. The fact that all bases share the same accuracy levels suggests that the learning pattern is a feature of the Collatz sequence.

4.1 The learning pattern – Correct predictions in different bases

Models using different bases not only achieve the same accuracy levels, they also succeed and fail on the same inputs. Consider the base-1515 and base-1717 models, which both achieve 81%81\% accuracy. If we test them on the same sample of 100,000 examples, we notice that they agree in 98%98\% of cases: they are both correct on 80,997 examples, and both wrong on 16,955. The two models disagree (one is correct, the other is wrong) on 2,048 examples, 2%2\% of the test set or about 10%10\% of model errors. This suggests that the steps in the learning pattern are associated with particular classes of inputs, that all models learn.

To characterize these classes, we calculate model accuracy on test examples that share a common residual modulo 2p2^{p}. For p=3p=3, we compare model performance on inputs of the form 8​k+18k+1, 8​k+38k+3, 8​k+58k+5 and 8​k+78k+7.

We notice that, for pp large enough, all residual classes modulo 2p2^{p} are either predicted with almost perfect accuracy (over 95%95\%), or not learned at all (less than 1%1\%). For instance, the base-1111 model achieves 99.9,99.999.9,99.9 and 96.6%96.6\% accuracy on inputs congruent to 11, 99 and 1111 modulo 1616, and less than 1%1\% on all other inputs (0.9%0.9\% for inputs congruent to 77, less than 0.1%0.1\% on other classes). This accounts for the 37%37\% accuracy reached by the base-1111 model. The nine models that achieve 55%55\% accuracy predict inputs congruent to 11 modulo 88, 1111 and 1313 modulo 1616 and 77 modulo 3232 with over 95%95\% accuracy, and all others with less than 1%1\%. This pattern is observed in all bases, throughout training. Accuracy jumps up when a new residual class is learned, and the order of learning is the same for all bases.

Residual classes modulo 2p2^{p} correspond to specific endings in the binary representation of inputs. Inputs congruent to 11 modulo 88 are the positive integers that have a binary representation ending in 0012001_{2}. Therefore, our base-1111 model has learned to predict inputs ending in 0012001_{2} and 101121011_{2} (and none others). Models with 55%55\% accuracy have learned two additional classes: inputs ending in 110121101_{2} and 00111200111_{2}, and models achieving 71%71\% accuracy (e.g. base 2121) predict three more: 00101200101_{2}, 10011210011_{2} and 1011112101111_{2}. The same pattern holds in even-base models: the base-5050 model, which achieves 92.3%92.3\% accuracy, predicts inputs ending in 01201_{2}, 0112011_{2}, 00111200111_{2}, 1011112101111_{2}, 1101112110111_{2}, 100111121001111_{2}, 101011121010111_{2}, 00010111200010111_{2} and 111000111121110001111_{2}.

This provides a complete account of the learning pattern. Every step in the learning curve happens when the model learns to predict (with near-perfect accuracy) a new class of inputs, characterized by their binary ending. All bases learn these classes in the same order, beginning with 0012001_{2}, 101121011_{2}, 110121101_{2}, 00111200111_{2} and 10011210011_{2}. Model accuracy is the frequency of these classes in the test set: twice the sum of the moduli, e.g. 2​(18+116)2(\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{16}) for base 1111. The learning pattern applies to all bases, but learning is faster in even bases, because the binary representation of inputs is easier to learn (all even numbers end in particular digits).

4.2 Why the binary classes – Learning k and k’

The learning pattern, common to all bases, appears to be a property of the long Collatz step. In fact, we will now show that the residual classes correspond to inputs nn associated with particular values of kk and k′k^{\prime}, the lengths of the two loops in the computation of κ⁡(n)\kappa(n). In other words, instead of learning the mapping

κ⁡(n)=(32)k​(n+1)−12k′,\kappa(n)=\frac{(\frac{3}{2})^{k}(n+1)-1}{2^{k^{\prime}}},

with kk and k′k^{\prime} functions of nn, the models learn its restriction to specific values of kk and k′k^{\prime}.

Let nn be an odd positive integer, and let BnB_{n} be its binary representation. We know from Section 3 that kk, the number of iterations in the first loop of the long Collatz step, is the number of 11s at the right of BnB_{n}. Thus, for any nn with k=1k=1, BnB_{n} must end in 0101, if k=2k=2, BnB_{n} must end in 011011, and so on.

Suppose k=1k=1, then BnB_{n} ends in 0101 and n=c0=4​m+1n=c_{0}=4m+1. Let us compute its long Collatz successor. After one iteration of the first loop (n→3​n+12n\to\frac{3n+1}{2}), we reach c1=3​n+12=6​m+2c_{1}=\frac{3n+1}{2}=6m+2, an even number. This is the apex: all future steps will be divisions by 22, k′≥1k^{\prime}\geq 1 is the largest power of two dividing c1c_{1}, and we have

κ⁡(n)=c1+k′=6​m+22k′.\kappa(n)=c_{1+k^{\prime}}=\frac{6m+2}{2^{k^{\prime}}}.

Dividing c1c_{1} by two yields c2=3​m+1c_{2}=3m+1. We now have two cases.

(1) If mm is even, c2=3​m+1c_{2}=3m+1 is odd. Then c2=κ⁡(n)c_{2}=\kappa(n) and k′=1k^{\prime}=1. Rewriting m=2​pm=2p, we have n=8​p+1n=8p+1. Therefore, BnB_{n} ends in 001001. This is the first class in the learning pattern, which contains all odd integers for which k=k′=1k=k^{\prime}=1.

(2) If mm is odd, we can write m=2​p+1m=2p+1 and BnB_{n} ends in 101101. Then c2=6​p+4c_{2}=6p+4, an even integer, so k′≥2k^{\prime}\geq 2, and c3=3​p+2c_{3}=3p+2. At this point, we again have two cases.

(2a) If pp is odd, c3=3​p+2c_{3}=3p+2 is odd, so c3=κ⁡(n)c_{3}=\kappa(n) and k′=2k^{\prime}=2. BnB_{n} ends in 11011101. This is the third class in the learning pattern: inputs for which k=1k=1 and k′=2k^{\prime}=2.

(2b) If pp is even, BnB_{n} ends in 01010101, c3=3​p+2=6​q+2c_{3}=3p+2=6q+2 is even, so k′≥3k^{\prime}\geq 3, and c4=3​q+1c_{4}=3q+1. We once again have two cases but since c4=3​q+1c_{4}=3q+1, they are the same as the ones we discussed for c2c_{2}, and the same reasoning applies.

Iterating, we see that, for inputs with k=1k=1, i.e. BnB_{n} ending in 0101, we have k′=1k^{\prime}=1 iff BnB_{n} ends in 001001, k′=2k^{\prime}=2 iff BnB_{n} ends in 11011101, k′=3k^{\prime}=3 iff BnB_{n} ends in 00101200101_{2}, and k′≥4k^{\prime}\geq 4 if BnB_{n} ends in 10101210101_{2}. By induction, we can prove that any k′k^{\prime} can be deduced from BnB_{n}, with the following rules:

  • •

    k′=2​p+1k^{\prime}=2p+1 if BnB_{n} ends in 0​(01)p​010(01)^{p}01 for some p≥0p\geq 0,

  • •

    k′=2​p+2k^{\prime}=2p+2 if BnB_{n} ends in 11​(01)p​0111(01)^{p}01 for some p≥0p\geq 0.

We can reformulate this as a general property of integers n≡1mod4n\equiv 1\mod 4.

Property 4.1.

Let n≡1mod4n\equiv 1\mod 4, its binary representation BnB_{n} ends in 0101. Consider the binary sequence S1=(01)p​01S_{1}=(01)^{p}01, with pp chosen large enough that S1S_{1} is longer than BnB_{n}, and let q≥2q\geq 2 be the longest matching suffix between BnB_{n} and S1S_{1}, then k=1k=1 and k′=q−1k^{\prime}=q-1.

This property is an instance of a more general theorem, valid for all kk, that we will state and prove. Let Φ⁡(n)\Phi(n) stand for the Euler function, |x||x| for the length of the binary sequence xx, and let addition of binary sequences stand for concatenation. We first prove the lemma.

Lemma 1.

For any l>0l>0, the sequence al,p=2−p⋅(3l−1)mod3la_{l,p}=2^{-p}\cdot(3^{l}-1)\mod 3^{l} is periodic, with period Φ⁡(3l)=3l−3l−1\Phi(3^{l})=3^{l}-3^{l-1}.

Proof.

Since 33 is prime, for any l≥1l\geq 1, the multiplicative group 𝒢=(ℤ/3l​ℤ)×\mathcal{G}=(\mathbb{Z}/3^{l}\mathbb{Z})^{\times} is cyclic, and has order Φ⁡(3l)\Phi(3^{l}). In fact, 𝒢\mathcal{G} includes all the positive integers up to 3l−13^{l}-1, co-prime with 3l3^{l}. Since 22 is a primitive root of 3l3^{l}, the sequence of remainders modulo 3l3^{l} of its positive powers, (2pmod3l)p≥0(2^{p}\mod 3^{l})_{p\geq 0}, generates 𝒢\mathcal{G}, as does the sequence of its negative powers (2−pmod3l)p≥0(2^{-p}\mod 3^{l})_{p\geq 0}. Finally, since 3l−13^{l}-1 is co-prime with 3l3^{l}, it is an element of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and (3l−1)​𝒢=𝒢(3^{l}-1)\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{G}. Therefore, the sequence (2−p⋅(3l−1)mod3l)p≥0(2^{-p}\cdot(3^{l}-1)\mod 3^{l})_{p\geq 0} generates 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and is periodic with period Φ⁡(3l)\Phi(3^{l}). ∎

Theorem 2.

Let HlH_{l} be the sequence of parities of (al,p)0≤p≤Φ⁡(3l)(a_{l,p})_{0\leq p\leq\Phi(3^{l})}, written in reverse order:

Hl,p=al,Φ⁡(3l)−p−1mod2,H_{l,p}=a_{l,\Phi(3^{l})-p-1}\mod 2,

Let nn be an odd positive integer larger than 11, with binary representation BnB_{n}. Let 2l2^{l} be the largest power of two dividing n+1n+1, and SlS_{l} the binary sequence Sl=(Hl)m​1lS_{l}=(H_{l})^{m}1^{l}, with mm chosen so that |Sl|>|Bn||S_{l}|>|B_{n}|, then

  1. i.

    BnB_{n} shares with SlS_{l} a common suffix of length s≥l+1s\geq l+1,

  2. ii.

    the long Collatz step of nn verifies k=lk=l and k′=s−lk^{\prime}=s-l.

Proof.

(i) For any ll, the rightmost bit of HlH_{l} is the parity of al,0=3l−1a_{l,0}=3^{l}-1, which is 00. Therefore, the rightmost l+1l+1 bits of SlS_{l} are 01l01^{l}. Theorem 2 states that, for any odd integer nn, the number of steps in the two loops of the long Collatz step calculation, kk and k′k^{\prime}, can be read from BnB_{n}, the binary representation of nn, by matching it with a family of binary sequences Sl=(Hl)p​1lS_{l}=(H_{l})^{p}1^{l}, for l>0l>0. The HlH_{l} are binary sequences of length Φ⁡(3l)\Phi(3^{l}), formed from the parities of the powers of 22 modulo 3l3^{l}. Their first values are H1=10H_{1}=10, H2=111000H_{2}=111000 and H3=111101101000010010H_{3}=111101101000010010. For instance, an integer with binary representation ending in 0000112000011_{2} must have k=2k=2, and since S2=(111000)p​11S_{2}=(111000)^{p}11, it matches S2S_{2} on the last s=5s=5 bits, so k′=5−3=3k^{\prime}=5-3=3. An integer with binary representation ending in 001101000010010111001101000010010111 (k=3k=3) matches the last 1717 bits of S3=(111101101000010010)p​111S_{3}=(111101101000010010)^{p}111, therefore k′=14k^{\prime}=14. SlS_{l} is the binary representation of an odd integer that has k=lk=l and k′k^{\prime} maximal. If the binary representation of nn matches the last p>lp>l bits of SlS_{l}, then k′≥p−lk^{\prime}\geq p-l.

The sequences HlH_{l} appear in other works on the Collatz conjecture. Colussi (2011) relates them with the convergence classes of the Collatz sequence: integers reaching 11 after ll iterations of the transformation n→(3​n+1)/2hn\to(3n+1)/2^{h}. Stérin (2020) relates them with the Collatz ancestors of particular integers.

Most importantly, theorem 2 provides an explanation for the learning pattern. For any pair (k,k′)(k,k^{\prime}), all odd integers nn for which

κ⁡(n)=(32)k​(n+1)−12k′\kappa(n)=\frac{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{k}(n+1)-1}{2^{k^{\prime}}}

share a binary suffix, the k+k′+1k+k^{\prime}+1 last bits of SkS_{k}. For k=k′=1k=k^{\prime}=1, this common suffix is 0012001_{2}, for k=1k=1, k′=2k^{\prime}=2, it is 110121101_{2}, for k=2k=2, k′=1k^{\prime}=1, it is 101121011_{2}. Every class in the learning pattern corresponds to a specific pair (k,k′)(k,k^{\prime}): the learning pattern amounts to learning the long Collatz step one pair (k,k′)(k,k^{\prime}) at a time.

  • •

    Models achieving 25%25\% accuracy (B=3B=3) have learned to predict the long Collatz successors for (k,k′)=(1,1)(k,k^{\prime})=(1,1) (25%25\% of all input).

  • •

    Models achieving 37%37\% accuracy (B=11B=11) predict (1,1)(1,1) and (2,1)(2,1) (37.5%37.5\% of input).

  • •

    Models achieving 55%55\% accuracy (B=5,13,19,29,35,37,53B=5,13,19,29,35,37,53) predict (1,1)(1,1), (2,1)(2,1), (1,2)(1,2) and (3,1)(3,1), (56.25%56.25\% of input).

Notice that classes are learned in increasing order of k+k′k+k^{\prime}, a consequence of Theorem 2.

Corollary 3.

Over all odd positive integers, the random variables kk and k′k^{\prime} are independent and their distribution verifies:

𝒫⁡(k=a)=12a,\mathcal{P}(k=a)=\frac{1}{2^{a}},
𝒫⁡(k′=b|k=a)=12b,\mathcal{P}(k^{\prime}=b|k=a)=\frac{1}{2^{b}},
𝒫⁡(k=a,k′=b)=12a+b.\mathcal{P}(k=a,k^{\prime}=b)=\frac{1}{2^{a+b}}.

Since kk and k′k^{\prime} can be read from BnB_{n}, it comes to no surprise that models using power-of-two bases learn best, and that even-base models perform better than odd-base models.

5 Patterns of model failures

In the previous section, we considered the inputs that are correctly predicted, and noticed that they correspond to integers associated with small values of kk and k′k^{\prime}. For these nn, the model correctly predicts κ⁡(n)\kappa(n). We now turn to model failures: inputs nn that are not predicted as κ⁡(n)\kappa(n).

Many prior works on transformers described hallucination: models outputting irrelevant predictions when they fail. This phenomenon is well-documented in large language models, pre-trained without supervision on large text corpora. Prior work suggests that math transformers, smaller models trained with supervision, do not hallucinate. Models trained to predict the eigen decomposition of symmetric real matrices predict, even when they fail, the correct eigenvalues, and unitary, albeit non-orthogonal, eigenvectors in most cases (Charton, 2022). Errors in models trained to predict GCD can be explained by three deterministic rules (Charton, 2024b).

For the long Collatz step, we will show that most model errors can be ascribed to a small number of predictable cases. In fact, we will propose a generalized version of the learning pattern that accounts for most model predictions: almost all correct predictions, and about 90%90\% of errors. In all experiments, we investigate the predictions of trained models on a test set of 100,000 examples. For each input nn, we compare the model prediction pp to the target value t=κ⁡(n)t=\kappa(n), and especially investigate the distribution of the ratio r=p/tr=p/t.

5.1 Errors in the best performing models

Let us first consider the models using bases 2424 and 3232. They achieve 99.7%99.7\% accuracy, 243243 and 265265 errors, respectively, on a test set of 100,000. As expected, the models fail for large values of kk and k′k^{\prime}. In base 2424, inputs with k≥11k\geq 11 are never correctly predicted, and only 43%43\% of inputs with k=10k=10 are correctly predicted. For k=9k=9, there are 1414 errors and 4141 correct predictions for k′=1k^{\prime}=1, 2626 errors and 55 correct predictions for k′=2k^{\prime}=2. For k′≥3k^{\prime}\geq 3, all predictions are incorrect. In base 3232, all inputs with k>9k>9 are incorrectly predicted, and account for 212212 of 265265 errors. Inputs with k=9k=9 account for 3939, almost all remaining errors.

In almost all errors, the ratio r=p/tr=p/t is very close to 11. In base 2424, 93%93\% of incorrect predictions (225225 out of 245245) are within 3%3\% of the correct value of κ⁡(n)\kappa(n), 84%84\% (204204) are within 1%1\% and 46%46\% (111111) within 0.1%0.1\%. In base 3232, 93%93\% (247247) are within 1%1\% of κ⁡(n)\kappa(n). Whereas these failures happen for the same inputs nn, model predictions vary for different bases.

We investigate these close misses by comparing the sequence predicted by the model (the base-BB representation of pp) with the base-BB representation of κ⁡(n)\kappa(n). In most cases, they agree on more than half of the digits: the beginning and end of the two sequences are the same. For example, in base-2424, the model predicts [4, 21, 20, 6, 7, 8, 8, 2, 20, 1] instead of [4, 21, 20, 6, 7, 3, 20, 2, 20, 1]: the five first and three last digits are correct. Incorrect predictions are not only close to the target values, but they share the same residuals modulo 24p24^{p} for small values of pp.

These observations generalize to all bases where models achieve high accuracy. Table 2 presents, for bases divisible by 88 or 1212, the average discrepancy between correct and predicted sequences for all model errors. On average, about half of the tokens are correct, evenly shared between the beginning and the end of the sequence. These results indicate that models errors are not random hallucinations, and suggest that the models do a better job at predicting the long Collatz step than their accuracy figures suggest.

5.2 Power-of-two errors in odd-base models

The long Collatz successor of an odd integer is always odd. In even-base models, this property is respected. All model prediction for bases 2424 and 3232 are odd. The largest number of even predictions, in an even-base models is 843843 for base 3838: 0.8%0.8\% of model predictions, and less than 5%5\% of errors. In an even base, the parity of outputs is easy to learn and control, as it only depends on the last token in the predicted sequence (which can only take values on half of the vocabulary).

No such shortcut for parity exists in odd bases22 2 Rules for parity testing exist in odd bases, but they require a weighted modular sum over all digits, a task transformers struggle on (Saxena et al., 2025)., and parity errors in odd-base models are frequent. In fact, they are too frequent. In base 2727 (71%71\% accuracy), 25%25\% of test set predictions (25,082 out of 100,000) are even, and account for 88%88\% of model errors (all even predictions are errors). Similar proportions are found for other odd bases (85%85\% for bases 2525 and 2929, 87%87\% for base 3131). The prevalence of even predictions in odd-base model is very surprising: a model guessing parity at random would only produce 50%50\% even predictions.

A look at the ratio r=p/tr=p/t settles this curious case. In about 70%70\% of model failures (Table 3), the ratio is exactly equal to a small power of 22. Instead of predicting t=κ⁡(n)t=\kappa(n), the model predicts, 2​κ​(n)2\kappa(n), 4​κ​(n)4\kappa(n) or 8​κ​(n)8\kappa(n), that is, while predicting the long Collatz step, k′k^{\prime}, the number of iterations in the second loop, is underestimated by a few units.

These power-of-two errors happen for specific values of nn, associated with kk that the models can predict (i.e. inputs with k′=1k^{\prime}=1 are correctly predicted for this kk), but large k′k^{\prime}, that are predicted as the largest value the model can predict. For instance, in base 2727, the model correctly predicts inputs with k=1k=1 and k′≤3k^{\prime}\leq 3, k=2k=2 and k′≤2k^{\prime}\leq 2, and k=3k=3 or 44 and k′=1k^{\prime}=1. Almost all (99.9%99.9\%) power-of-two errors happen for inputs with k=1,k′≥4k=1,k^{\prime}\geq 4, k=2,k′≥3k=2,k^{\prime}\geq 3, and k=3k=3 or 44 and k′≥2k^{\prime}\geq 2 (and 99%99\% of model predictions for these inputs are power-of-two errors). In all power-of-two errors, the model predicts k′=3k^{\prime}=3 for k=1k=1, k′=2k^{\prime}=2 for k=2k=2 and k′=1k^{\prime}=1 for k=3k=3 or 44.

In other words, power-of-two errors happen for values of kk that the model can predict correctly up to a certain value of k′=lk′k^{\prime}=l_{k}^{\prime}. Inputs associated with this value of kk are predicted as p=2k′−lk′​κ​(n)p=2^{k^{\prime}-l_{k}^{\prime}}\kappa(n) (the largest k′k^{\prime} that the model has learned so far).

These observations apply to all odd bases. In base 99 (83%83\% accuracy), models correctly predict inputs with kk up to 55. Power-of-two errors happen for k=1k=1 and k′≥5k^{\prime}\geq 5 (the model then predicts p=2k′−4​κ​(n)p=2^{k^{\prime}-4}\kappa(n)), k=2k=2 and k′≥4k^{\prime}\geq 4 (predicting p=2k′−3​κ​(n)p=2^{k^{\prime}-3}\kappa(n)), k=3k=3 and k′≥3k^{\prime}\geq 3 (p=2k′−2​κ​(n)p=2^{k^{\prime}-2}\kappa(n)), and k=4k=4 or 55 and k′≥2k^{\prime}\geq 2 (p=2k′−1​κ​(n)p=2^{k^{\prime}-1}\kappa(n)). In base 1111 (37%37\% accuracy), inputs with k=1k=1, k′=1k^{\prime}=1 and k=2k=2, k′=1k^{\prime}=1 are correctly predicted, all other inputs with k≤2k\leq 2 are power-of-two-errors, predicted as p=2k′−1​κ​(n)p=2^{k^{\prime}-1}\kappa(n). Inputs with k>2k>2 are almost never correct predictions or power-of-two errors.

Power-of-two errors generalize the learning pattern, for odd-base models. For every model, there exists a value kmaxk_{\text{max}}, the largest kk for which inputs associated with the pair (kmax,1)(k_{\text{max}},1) are predicted with high accuracy. For 1≤k≤kmax1\leq k\leq k_{\text{max}}, let lk′l_{k}^{\prime} be the largest value of k′k^{\prime} that the model can predict, then almost all inputs with k′≤lk′k^{\prime}\leq l_{k}^{\prime} are correctly predicted, and almost all inputs with k′>lk′k^{\prime}>l_{k}^{\prime} are power-of-two errors, predicted as p=2k′−lk′​κ​(n)p=2^{k^{\prime}-l_{k}^{\prime}}\kappa(n).

Almost all inputs associated with k>kmaxk>k_{\text{max}} are neither correct prediction, nor power-of-two errors. We call these hard errors. On these, model predictions are even in about 50%50\% of cases. Therefore, power-of-two errors account for the larger number of even predictions in odd-models.

Once again, these results indicate that the model does a much better job at learning κ⁡(n)\kappa(n) than its accuracy suggests. For almost all inputs with k≤kmaxk\leq k_{\text{max}}, the model predicts κ⁡(n)\kappa(n) up to a predictable power-of-two factor. For base 2727, these account for 93%93\% of model predictions. For base 1919, they account for 87%87\%.

5.3 Near power-of-two errors in even bases

Figures 3 and 3 present the distribution of ratios (r=p/tr=p/t) for all errors in base 2626 and 3838. Like accuracy levels, ratios concentrate around a small number of discrete values. Most of the ratios are very close to powers of two, r≈2lr\approx 2^{l}, with l≥1l\geq 1. They are distributed as a power law: 𝒫⁡(r≈2l)=K2l\mathcal{P}(r\approx 2^{l})=\frac{K}{2^{l}}. This is observed in all even bases, except those divisible by large powers of two, discussed in Section 5.1.

Only a small fraction of these errors are power-of-two errors, that is, verify p=2l​tp=2^{l}t. Such exact power-of-two errors account for 328328 errors out of 1067510675 in base 2626, and 561561 out of 1680816808 in base 3838. All others are near power-of-two errors (NP2E), which verify p=2l​κ​(n)+ϵp=2^{l}\kappa(n)+\epsilon, for ϵ\epsilon a small odd integer. We consider that all predictions verifying ϵ/p<0.001\epsilon/p<0.001 are NP2E. NP2E account for 56%56\% of model errors in base 2626 (60046004 out of 1067510675), 64%64\% in base 2222, and 67%67\% in base 3838. They are the first cause of errors in non-power-of-two even-base models.

All κ⁡(n)\kappa(n) in the training set are odd. In an even base, it means that all output sequences end with an odd digit. This inductive bias is learned by the model. Therefore, in almost all NP2E, the model predicts (wrongly) an odd integer, and ϵ\epsilon, which appears as a “rounding error” forced upon the model by the inductive bias, is odd. The distribution of ϵ\epsilon is not random. In base 2626, |ϵ||\epsilon| takes the values 1,131,13 and 132=16913^{2}=169 in 80%80\% of NP2E. In base 3838, it takes the values 1,191,19 and 19219^{2}, and in base 2222, the values 1,111,11 and 11211^{2}. Whereas the error pattern is a property of the long Collatz step, model predictions depend on the base.

In another common error pattern, the ratio r=p/tr=p/t has the form 2lB\frac{2^{l}}{B}. In these NP2E errors, the last odd digit in the output sequence is replaced by the <end-of-sentence> (EOS) token, and the output is cut short. In base 2626, we have r≈2lBr\approx\frac{2^{l}}{B} in 23222322 cases (23%23\% of errors), and r≈2lB2r\approx\frac{2^{l}}{B^{2}} in 215215 cases (2%2\% of errors). In base 2222, these account for 1616 and 2%2\% of errors, in base 3838 for 1010 and 1%1\%.

Overall, near power-of-two errors account for 81%81\% of model errors for base 2626, 82%82\% for base 2222 and 78%78\% for base 3838. The proportion of NP2E in even bases is similar to the proportion of power-of-two errors in odd bases.

All NP2E follow the same learning pattern as power-of-two errors in odd bases. For an input nn, with loop lengths kk and k′k^{\prime}, let kmaxk_{\text{max}} be the largest kk that the model can predict correctly, and let, for any k≤kmaxk\leq k_{\text{max}}, lk′l_{k}^{\prime} be the largest value of k′k^{\prime} that the model predicts for that value of kk. All NP2E happen when k≤kmaxk\leq k_{\text{max}} and k′>lk′k^{\prime}>l_{k}^{\prime}, and the power-of-two associated with the NP2E is 2k′−lk′2^{k^{\prime}-l_{k}^{\prime}}. In base 2626, NP2E represent 97.5%97.5\% of model errors for inputs with k≤kmaxk\leq k_{\text{max}} and k′>lk′k^{\prime}>l^{\prime}_{k}.

5.4 Hard errors

Power-of-two errors, exact or near, account for about 80%80\% of all model errors, and almost all errors for inputs with k≤kmaxk\leq k_{\text{max}}, for all bases except the best performing. We now investigate the remaining hard errors. Figures 5 to 7 present the distribution of p/tp/t for hard errors, for bases 26,38,2726,38,27 and 1919. The distributions are discrete, and take values of the form r≈(23)a​2lr\approx(\frac{2}{3})^{a}2^{l} with probability

𝒫⁡(r≈(23)a​2l)=K2l,\mathcal{P}(r\approx(\frac{2}{3})^{a}2^{l})=\frac{K}{2^{l}},

for small positive values of aa and l≥0l\geq 0. For base 2727, we also find ratios of the form r≈(23)a​2lBr\approx(\frac{2}{3})^{a}\frac{2^{l}}{B}.

Just as the power-of-two errors happen when the model underestimates k′k^{\prime}, these hard errors correspond to situations when kk is underestimated as k−ak-a.

In base 2626, we have kmax=6k_{\text{max}}=6, and k>kmaxk>k_{\text{max}} in 15451545 test examples, all predicted incorrectly. There are 3636 close misses, 3636 near power-of-two errors, and 14731473 hard errors. We have p≈23​2l​tp\approx\frac{2}{3}2^{l}t (kk underestimated by 11) in 607607 cases, and p≈23​B​2l​tp\approx\frac{2}{3B}2^{l}t (kk underestimated by 11, and the sequence truncated by one token) in 3131. These account for 43%43\% of hard errors. kk is underestimated by 22 in 319319 cases (22%22\% of hard errors), by 33 in 185185, by 44 in 6565, &c.

In all cases, the model predicts (up to factor BB) as if k=kmaxk=k_{\text{max}} and k′=1k^{\prime}=1, and

p≈(32)6​(n+1)−12,p\approx\frac{(\frac{3}{2})^{6}(n+1)-1}{2},

this accounts for 82%82\% or hard errors, but most of the remaining 289289 errors follow similar patterns. In 6666 cases, the model predicts as if k=7k=7 and k′=1k^{\prime}=1, in 1313 k=8k=8 and k′=1k^{\prime}=1, in 88, k=6k=6 and k′=2k^{\prime}=2. All model predictions correspond to incorrect guesses of kk and k′k^{\prime}.

This error pattern is observed in all bases. For base 3838 (kmax=5k_{\text{max}}=5), the model predicts k=5k=5, k′=1k^{\prime}=1 (up to a division by BB) in 86%86\% of hard errors. In base 1919 (kmax=3k_{\text{max}}=3), the same pattern accounts for 90%90\% of hard errors. In base 2727 (kmax=3k_{\text{max}}=3), it accounts for 92%92\%.

Summarizing, for inputs with k>kmaxk>k_{\text{max}}, 8080 to 95%95\% of hard errors (depending on the base) are due to the model predicting k=kmaxk=k_{\text{max}} and k′=1k^{\prime}=1. Infrequently, the model prediction is cut by one (rarely two) tokens.

5.5 A hierarchy of errors – the learning pattern revisited

This analysis of failure cases provides a broader perspective on the learning pattern. It appears that instead of learning κ⁡(n)\kappa(n) for all nn, or an approximation of it, all models learn a collection of functions κk,k′\kappa_{k,k^{\prime}}, that are equal to κ\kappa over integers nn associated with kk and k′k^{\prime}.

In other words, instead of learning the function

κ⁡(n)=(32)k⁡(n)​(n+1)−12k′​(n),\kappa(n)=\frac{(\frac{3}{2})^{k(n)}(n+1)-1}{2^{k^{\prime}(n)}},

where k⁡(n)k(n) and k′​(n)k^{\prime}(n) can be derived from the binary representation of nn, as in Section 4.2, the model learns a sequence of functions

κl,l′​(n)=(32)l​(n+1)−12l′,\kappa_{l,l^{\prime}}(n)=\frac{(\frac{3}{2})^{l}(n+1)-1}{2^{l^{\prime}}},

derived from κ\kappa by replacing the functions k⁡(n)k(n) and k′​(n)k^{\prime}(n) by the constants ll and l′l^{\prime}. We have κ​(n)=κl,l′​(n)\kappa(n)=\kappa_{l,l^{\prime}}(n) for all nn in

𝒟l,l′={n=2p+1,p∈ℕ∣k(n)=l,k′(n)=l′}.\mathcal{D}_{l,l^{\prime}}=\{n=2p+1,p\in\mathbb{N}\mid k(n)=l,k^{\prime}(n)=l^{\prime}\}.

When training begins, the model predicts for all nn an approximation of

κ1,1​(n)=32​(n+1)−12.\kappa_{1,1}(n)=\frac{\frac{3}{2}(n+1)-1}{2}.

This is equal to κ⁡(n)\kappa(n) on 𝒟1,1\mathcal{D}_{1,1}, resulting in an accuracy of 25%25\%.

As training progresses, new values of kk and k′k^{\prime} are learned, in increasing order of k+k′k+k^{\prime}. Once the model has learned all kk up to kmaxk_{\text{max}}, and all k′k^{\prime} up to lk′l_{k}^{\prime} for a given value of kk, it predicts (exactly) κk,k′​(n)=κ​(n)\kappa_{k,k^{\prime}}(n)=\kappa(n) for all nn such that k≤kmaxk\leq k_{\text{max}} and k′≤l′​(k)k^{\prime}\leq l^{\prime}(k) (all nn in 𝒟k,k′\mathcal{D}_{k,k^{\prime}}). For larger k<kmaxk<k_{\text{max}} and k′>lk′k^{\prime}>l_{k}^{\prime}, the model predicts κk,lk′​(n)\kappa_{k,l_{k}^{\prime}}(n). For k>kmaxk>k_{\text{max}}, it predicts κkmax,1​(n)\kappa_{k_{\text{max}},1}(n). These calculations are approximate, and subject to rounding errors. In a small number of cases, the model predicts 1B​κk,k′​(n)\frac{1}{B}\kappa_{k,k^{\prime}}(n), or 1B2​κk,k′​(n)\frac{1}{B^{2}}\kappa_{k,k^{\prime}}(n).

These rules account for more than 99%99\% of model predictions for k≤kmaxk\leq k_{\text{max}}, and 8585 to 95%95\% for k>kmaxk>k_{\text{max}}. Therefore, the updated learning pattern provide an almost complete explanation of model predictions.

6 Ablation studies

We now investigate a number of questions raised by the experiments from Section 4. We first consider simpler versions of the problem: learning the first loop of the algorithm (predicting the apex instead of the long Collatz successor), and learning the loop lengths (predicting k⁡(n)k(n) and k′​(n)k^{\prime}(n)). We then investigate the hypothesis that models learn the long Collatz step by first learning to translate their input into binary representation. Finally, we study the impact of different training distributions.

6.1 Simpler versions of the problem: predicting the apex and the loop lengths

The long Collatz step is a complex arithmetic operation. It features two loops of variable lengths, k⁡(n)k(n) and k′​(n)k^{\prime}(n), that the model must learn to compute the long step. We now consider two simpler versions of this task: predicting the apex ck=(32)k​(n+1)−1c_{k}={(\frac{3}{2})}^{k}(n+1)-1, which amounts to computing the first loop only, and predicting the lengths of the loops, the pair (k,k′)(k,k^{\prime}). We train models with the same architecture and number of parameters as in the main experiments, on random odd integers from 11 to 101210^{12}, encoded in base 22 to 5757.

Learning the first loop.

On this simple task, model accuracies are higher on average than when learning κ⁡(n)\kappa(n), the long Collatz successor (Table 4). Even-base models perform better than odd-base models, and the best performances are achieved by bases multiples of 1212. Learning curves (Figure 8) keep their step-like shape, and accuracy levels take a few quantized values, close to 1−12n1-\frac{1}{2^{n}} (50,75,87.5,93.8,96.8,98.4,99.2,99.6,99.8%50,75,87.5,93.8,96.8,98.4,99.2,99.6,99.8\%). This suggests a learning pattern where models learn to predict all input up to a certain kk.

An analysis of model errors confirms this hypothesis. Base-1313 models (50%50\% accuracy) predict p=3​n+12p=\frac{3n+1}{2} for almost all nn, as if k=1k=1 for all nn. Models with 75%75\% accuracy (e.g. base 2121) predict p=3​n+12p=\frac{3n+1}{2} for k=1k=1 and p=9​n+54p=\frac{9n+5}{4} for k≥2k\geq 2. Models with 87.5%87.5\% accuracy predict all k≤3k\leq 3 and so on. The best models predict all inputs with kk up to 99.

Interestingly, there is no qualitative difference between models trained to predict the long Collatz step and models trained to predict the apex. The presence of only one loop, the length of which is easier to read from the binary representation of nn, does not result in a different learning pattern.

Learning loop lengths.

Predicting kk and k′k^{\prime} eliminates the arithmetic calculations in the task. The model no longer needs to learn the transformations n→3​n+12n\to\frac{3n+1}{2} and n→n2n\to\frac{n}{2}, and the task becomes a pattern recognition problem: identifying the class (k,k′)(k,k^{\prime}) associated with the input nn (from a small set of possible classes). We know from Section 4.2 that this can be deduced from the k+k′+1k+k^{\prime}+1 rightmost bits in the binary representation of nn.

The learning curves are step-shaped and accuracy take quantized levels that roughly correspond to those observed when predicting κ⁡(n)\kappa(n) (Figure 9). Models using base 2,4,8,162,4,8,16 or 3232 achieve 100%100\% accuracy. In these bases, kk and k′k^{\prime} can be read from the (binary) input sequence. Base-4848 and 2424 models achieve almost perfect accuracies (99.9999.99 and 99.9899.98), but all other bases perform worse than when predicting the long Collatz successor. In particular, odd-base models fail to learn the task and achieve 25%25\% accuracy by always predicting the most frequent outcome, kk=k′k^{\prime}=11. Even-base models not a power of 22 or divisible by 2424 reach higher accuracies, but always perform worse than when predicting κ⁡(n)\kappa(n). For instance, base-3030 and base-4646 models achieve 56%56\% accuracy, vs 89%89\% for κ⁡(n)\kappa(n).

The learning pattern applies: kk and k′k^{\prime} are learned in increasing order of k+k′k+k^{\prime}, yielding the familiar quantized accuracy levels at 2525, 3737, 5656, 7171, 8181, 8888, and 91%91\% (Table 5). However, a fine structure appears, as accuracy levels split into bands of close, quantized values, where the largest correct values of k′k^{\prime} are predicted with less than 99%99\% accuracy.

For instance, models using bases 1414, 5050 and 5454 achieve 72%72\% accuracy by predicting all inputs with k=1k=1, k′≤4k^{\prime}\leq 4, k=2k=2, k′≤2k^{\prime}\leq 2 and k=3,4k=3,4, k′=1k^{\prime}=1, with over 98%98\% accuracy. Base-3434 and 2222 models predict the same pairs, but (1,3)(1,3), (2,2)(2,2) and (4,1)(4,1) are predicted with 95%95\% accuracy only, for a model performance of 71.5%71.5\%. In the base-3838 model these three pairs are predicted with 90%90\% accuracy, for a performance of 70%70\%, and in base 4646 and 3030 with 75%75\%, for a performance of 69%69\%. These suggest a second-order mechanism for the learning of new (k,k′)(k,k^{\prime}) classes. Here, all three classes are learned simultaneously, but in discrete steps.

The lower performance of models learning to predict kk and k′k^{\prime}, compared to models predicting κ⁡(n)\kappa(n), is very counter-intuitive. One would expect that a simpler task – predicting loop lengths – is easier to learn than a complex one – predicting loop lengths AND calculating κ⁡(n)\kappa(n). We believe that the behavior of odd-base models, that easily learn the obvious solution k=k′=1k=k^{\prime}=1, for 25%25\% accuracy, but never get out of the local minimum of the loss function, offer insight about what is happening. In this task, the model is tasked to predict two small integers, when predicting k=k′=1k=k^{\prime}=1, from uniformly distributed inputs, the model is correct on both tokens, i.e. the cross-entropy loss is zero, in 25%25\% of cases, but the model predicts at least one integer right in 75%75\% of training examples. This suggests a very flat loss landscape around the local minimum, which becomes very hard to escape. The same observation can be made for larger accuracy levels: because the distribution of kk and k′k^{\prime} are independent and exponentially decreasing, the loss function is very flat around local minima. In contrast, when predicting κ⁡(n)\kappa(n), there is no obvious solution, that would result in flat local minima. This empirical observation deserves further story: it suggests that simple but hard-to-learn arithmetic functions may be easier to learn if they are “relaxed” into harder (regression) problems. Here, even if the goal is to learn kk and k′k^{\prime}, on would prefer to train a model to predict κ⁡(n)\kappa(n), from which kk ad k′k^{\prime} can be deduced.

6.2 Can transformers learn base conversion?

The long Collatz step is easier to learn when inputs and outputs are encoded in a base divisible by a large power of 22. In such bases, the rightmost bits in the binary representation of nn, which encode the loop lengths kk and k′k^{\prime} (Section 4.2), can be deduced from the last tokens in the input sequence (specifically, if BB is a multiple of 2d2^{d}, the pp last bits in BnB_{n} are encoded in the ⌈pd⌉\lceil\frac{p}{d}\rceil last digits of the sequence representing nn).

This suggests a possible explanation for the accuracy gaps between different bases. Models might first learn to convert their input into binary representation, then learn the long Collatz step. The worse performance of odd-models would then be a consequence of the additional work of learning to convert model input into their binary representation. For output bases, we selected 2,8,322,8,32 and 2424, the bases that achieved the best performance in our experiments from Section 4. For input base, we chose 4,12,22,36,42,56,3,9,27,11,15,13,314,12,22,36,42,56,3,9,27,11,15,13,31 and 4343. For each of these 5656 input/output pairs, two models were trained over a random training set of 700700 million integers from 11 to 101210^{12}.

The results were very disappointing: only 88 models out of 108108 achieved an accuracy of 98%98\% or more: the 66 models converting base 44 into base 2,82,8 and 3232, and the 22 models converting base 1212 into 2424. The two models converting base 44 into 2424 achieved 47%47\% accuracy, and models converting base 3636 into 2424 achieved 1111 and 1%1\%. All other models achieved less than 0.2%0.2\% accuracy. Models only learn to convert in the trivial case where one base is a multiple of the other.

These results refute our hypothesis, by demonstrating that base conversion is a hard task for transformers. They also confirm the surprising nature of our results on odd-base models. The learning pattern clearly indicates that odd-base models learn to classify inputs according to their binary ending (i.e. their residuals modulo 2p2^{p}), but our experiments demonstrate that learning the binary representation of a number from its digits in an odd-base sequence is a hard task.

6.3 Training from different distributions

Corollary 3 from Section 4.2 offer a possible explanation for the learning pattern. Since the probability of a uniformly distributed input nn being associated with kk and k′k^{\prime} is 2−(k+k′)2^{-(k+k^{\prime})}, inputs nn associated with k=k′=1k=k^{\prime}=1, the first class in the learning pattern, account for 25%25\% the training set. The second class (k=2k=2, k′=1k^{\prime}=1) account for 12.5%12.5\%, inputs with k=k′=3k=k^{\prime}=3 for 1.5625%1.5625\%, and inputs with k≥5k\geq 5 for 6.25%6.25\%. Thus, the learning pattern might just be a consequence of the distribution of training data, and large values of kk and k′k^{\prime} would be hard to learn because they are less common. Such a situation was observed in previous work (Charton, 2024b), and large increases in performance could be achieved by training the model on a more balanced distribution.
